verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that the distant demonstrative “those” marks the Qurʾan’s lofty, exalted status as God’s word sent down to earth. Here āyāt means the constituent, recited parts of divine speech: verses distinguished from one another by their meanings, which accounts for scholarly disagreements over the verse counts of some sūrahs.

“The Wise Book” means a scripture in which wisdom is firmly established. If ḥakīm is understood in the passive sense of muḥkam, it means a book secure from corruption or refutation. In either sense, it is the Qurʾan revealed to the Prophet.

Although the view that the Wise Book is the Guarded Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), from which Qurʾanic verses descend, has merit, the apparent sense of this verse and similar openings is that the Book and its signs are the Qurʾan and its humanly recited verses. The Qurʾan is thus like a book taken from the protected Book, which is immune from falsehood and corruption.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan holds that the opening question rebukes people for finding it strange that God revealed the Qurʾanic message to a human being from among themselves. The revelation commands him to warn all mankind, while giving glad tidings specifically to the faithful. Thus the Qurʾan harms those who persist in disbelief and disobedience, but benefits those who believe and obey.

The promised qadam ṣidqin, “good standing,” is the abode or rank of truthfulness with God. Faith that brings nearness to God and a high rank with Him is truthful faith, and its possessor attains the abode of truthfulness. Qadam, literally “foot,” is figuratively a station or rank; the phrase denotes a standing belonging to one distinguished by honesty. Another explanation portrays honesty as having a firm foot that does not slip, unlike dishonesty.

The faithless either call the Prophet “a plain magician,” or, in an alternative recitation, call the Qurʾan “plain magic.” The meaning in both is that they accuse the Prophet of working magic through the Qurʾan. It appears that their astonishment arises because its speech differs strikingly from their own, is evidently miraculous, and profoundly affects hearts and minds.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse answers the idolaters’ rejection of revelation and their charge that the Qurʾan is magic. It begins to establish that the Prophet’s message and the Qurʾan’s teachings are true and must be followed.

God created the heavens and earth in six stages, then established Himself upon the Throne of divine power and assumed governance of the cosmos, to which all created affairs return. Because He governs without helper or supporter, nothing can intervene in creation’s affairs except by His permission. This is the meaning of intercession (shafāʿa): God is the First Cause, above which there is no cause, while every lesser cause is caused by Him and can intercede only by His leave.

Consequently, God alone is the people’s Lord and governor, not the beings they have adopted as lords or intercessors beside Him. The command to worship Him calls them to reflect on divinity, creation, and governance and recognize that no lord exists besides God.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains that “Allah’s true promise” means that God has truthfully promised the Return and Resurrection. Since ḥaqq is a statement corresponding to reality, the promise is true because creation is not complete until all things, including human beings, return to God. As a falling stone necessarily continues until it reaches the earth, all things move toward their Lord until they meet Him.

“Indeed He originates the creation, then He will bring it back” both emphasizes the Return and supplies a proof of Resurrection. God grants creatures existence and mercy until their appointed term, but their end is not annihilation. The mercy by which they subsist, with life, power, and knowledge, remains in God’s omnipotent hand; what He pours into creation remains His countenance and does not perish. Their end is therefore their return to God’s presence, just as they came from it: creation and return are God’s expansion and contraction of being, through unfurling and seizing His mercy.

The verse also proves Resurrection through divine justice. God will not treat faithful doers of righteous deeds as equal to those who arrogantly deny Him and His signs, even though both are subject in this world to the same natural order of benefit and harm. After their return, He will distinguish them: the faithful receive enjoyable reward, while the faithless receive painful punishment. Grammatically, “that He may reward” may qualify either the universal Return or His bringing creation back; the latter is more likely, though the proof remains the same.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that God made the sun a source of radiance and the moon a source of light, and appointed the moon’s successive phases. As it advances night by night and then returns, its course measures the lunar month, enabling calculation of months and years.

The verse is a proof of God’s exclusive Lordship. The sun and moon serve the needs of earthly creatures, and the moon’s phases provide beneficial reckoning. Their order has real purposes within the natural order God created: nothing in it is vain, false, or a chance coincidence. God arranged creation to govern human affairs in this world and the next; therefore, no lord exists besides Him.

“Signs” may mean either the signs of creation in the external world or those in revealed scripture, though the former better suits the context.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan states that ikhtilāf, originally connected with one thing turning its back on another and then extended to every kind of difference, may describe night and day in two ways. It may mean their successive covering of the earth, producing weeks, months, and years; or their changing relative lengths across the seasons, with the northern and southern regions varying oppositely.

Their succession organizes earthly life: daylight brings the sun’s warmth and activity, while night brings darkness, coolness, rest, and dwelling. Their changing lengths produce the four seasons, through which provisions are brought forth. Nahār particularly denotes the period of daylight and is ordinarily contrasted with layl, whereas yawm more generally denotes a day.

The alternation of night and day, together with all creation in heaven and earth, is governed by one unified cosmic order that serves created beings, especially human life, in the best manner. It therefore provides a complete proof of the oneness of divine Lordship: God has no partner in it. The verse may also explain why God elaborates His signs for people of knowledge; if so, the more suitable meaning of ikhtilāf is the simple succession of night and day, in keeping with the preceding discussion of the sun, moon, and lunar phases.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses set out the consequence of rejecting the call to worship God. Those who do not expect to encounter God do not expect the Resurrection and Return to Him. They consequently deny recompense, moral accountability, promise and threat, commands and prohibitions; this invalidates revelation, prophethood, and divine religion as a whole.

Denying the Hereafter confines a person’s pursuit of survival and happiness to worldly life. Someone who believes in an enduring life embracing this world and the next seeks happiness in both; one who recognizes only this limited life is pleased with it and settles in it. Their satisfaction with the world follows from their failure to hope for the encounter with God, and their heedlessness of His signs explains both conditions.

Turning from God’s remembrance limits knowledge to worldly life, entails straying from God’s path, and amounts to forgetting the Day of Reckoning. Thus the criterion is remembrance of God and seeking the Hereafter: there is no difference between one who explicitly denies Resurrection and lives for this world, and one who effectively denies it through worldly conduct alone. Belief in Resurrection is a fundamental doctrine, without which the whole structure of religion collapses. Those characterized in this way will remain eternally in Hellfire because of the deeds they earned in the world.

verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that God guides the faithful, who respond to His call and perform righteous deeds, through their faith to their Lord. Guidance to truth, the straight path, or any other Qurʾanic destination consists of stages on the path whose final terminus is God Himself.

Though the verse joins faith (īmān) with righteous deeds (aʿmāl ṣāliḥa), it attributes this guidance and elevation to faith alone. Faith brings the servant to divine proximity, while righteous deeds support and enact faith. Righteous conduct, however, does contribute to earning Paradise’s blessings, just as sinful conduct contributes to deserved punishment.

The gardens and streams of the faithful signify the abode of nearness to God. In light of other verses, their blessings symbolize God’s guardianship (wilāya). God singles out His allies (awliyāʾ), who enjoy proximity to Him, for the wine and springs of Paradise; this displays His special concern for them.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s friends (awliyāʾ) are those whose hearts contain none but God and who entrust their affairs to none but Him. To ennoble them, God purifies their hearts from love of all besides Him, so that they love and attach themselves only to Him or for His sake, and are free of every partner or distraction that diverts them from His remembrance.

Their saying, “O Allah! Immaculate are You!” (subḥānaka), declares God transcendent above every unbefitting thing: partners, deficiency, and non-existence. Their glorification is enacted in deed as well as speech, since anything less remains tainted by a kind of polytheism. Their hearts, filled with God’s love and thus with goodness and peace, turn to others only with goodness and peace—except where those others turn this into evil and malediction.

Because they see every thing as God’s blessing and as a manifestation of His beautiful names, attributes, grandeur, and perfection, they do not describe anything while forgetting Him. Their every description therefore includes praise of God’s actions and attributes, for praise is lauding one for chosen actions.

When they meet their Lord, He fulfils His promise, admits them to His mercy and generosity, completes their light, and gives them a drink that purifies their hearts of manifest and hidden idolatry. Enveloped in the light of knowledge and certitude, they will have springs of divine unity flow from their hearts onto their tongues: first glorifying God, then greeting their companions among prophets, truthful ones, witnesses, and righteous people with peace, and finally praising God.

The flowing streams may thus describe the paradise of God’s guardianship (jannat al-wilāya) and their purification. Their glorification occurs in God’s presence, without a veil from Him; their greeting of “Peace” expresses Paradise’s absolute security; and their final praise follows their recognition of His beautiful names and attributes. This is the highest rank of Paradise’s inhabitants, reached through perfected knowledge of God.

The commentary adds that no creature can adequately describe God except His servants devoted wholly to worship, whose hearts are given to Him and whom He brings near without intermediary. The Qurʾan accordingly relates praise from its noblest prophets and from Paradise’s inhabitants. The verse promises that faithful believers will be joined in the Hereafter with God’s devoted servants, and thus gives them glad tidings of a beautiful divine reward.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that if God hastened punishment for people as they hasten to seek benefits and blessings, He would send down their punishment and end them. Taʿjīl means bringing something about quickly, while istiʿjāl is demanding speed; yaʿmahūn denotes intense confusion. The verse concerns deniers of the resurrection, who reject faith and wander bewildered in rebellion.

People impatiently seek the quickest route to what benefits them and, since all ultimate causation belongs to God, effectively demand such haste from Him. This self-driven habit is ignorant: the world’s causes do not conform to human whims, but people are subject to the cosmic order. Were the divine ordering of causes and effects to follow this ignorant human haste, divine punishment would swiftly annihilate them. Its basis lies in their own disbelief, denial of the Hereafter and encounter with God, and rebellion. Yet God’s process rests on wisdom, so He does not hasten their calamity but leaves defiant disbelievers in their confusion.

The phrase la-quḍiya ilayhim ajaluhum contains a kind of assurance: la-quḍiya, taking ilā, suggests that their appointed end would be conveyed or sent down upon them, a compound allusion to the descent of divine punishment. The shift from third-person reference to God to “We leave” perhaps indicates that such acts as leaving people bewildered, removing distress, and annihilating occur through the mediation of causes and effects, as rulers use “we” when their servants participate in an affair.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan states that ḍurr is harm affecting a person. Supplicating while on one’s side, sitting, or standing apparently conveys generality: in every condition, a person persists in calling upon God without forgetting. It is also possible that these are the states in which distress befalls the person rather than the modes of supplication. Some traditions with incomplete chains interpret them accordingly: lying on one’s side is the state of one too ill or injured to sit, sitting that of one unable to stand, and standing that of one who is healthy.

When God removes the affliction, the person goes on as though he had never called upon Him, neglecting and forgetting what cannot be forgotten. Thus, those who deny resurrection resemble one who remembers his Lord and repeatedly begs for relief in hardship, then returns to his former transgressions once relief comes. Their excessive attachment to worldly adornment makes their deeds appear alluring, so that they overlook divine lordship and forget God.

Al-Mizan further explains that Satan’s adorning of their sinful deeds captivates their hearts and leaves no room for remembering God. Even though previous messengers brought clear miracles, reminded them of God’s sovereignty, and drew attention to the destruction of earlier peoples for disbelief and wrongdoing, they refuse faith. This is the divine custom by which wrongdoers are punished, and the following verse, Certainly We destroyed generations before you (10:13), supplements this exposition.
verses.13: Al-Mizan notes that the shift from speaking of past peoples in the third person to addressing “you” in “before you” intensifies the verse’s warning, since a direct warning is more effective. The further shift in “Thus do We requite the guilty lot” addresses the Prophet: it sets out God’s established way of punishing the guilty, which he is especially suited to understand and to establish for others so that they will believe it rather than deny it. This differs from the preceding historical account, for belief or disbelief does not affect what has already occurred.
verses.14: Al-Mizan states that God’s testing of people is a continuous and universal divine custom throughout history.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters’ demand for another Qurʾan arose because its call to God’s oneness, rejection of idolatry, and prohibition of injustice and sin opposed their desires. To ask for another Qurʾan was to seek one without these teachings; to ask that it be altered was to retain its form while changing the meanings they disliked to suit their whims. They thus treated the Qurʾan like trivial entertainment that listeners may replace or revise at will.

The commentary rejects the view that “another” means adding a new Qurʾan alongside the present one, whereas “alter it” means removing it: the idolaters did not want both Qurʾans. It likewise rejects the claim that they merely sought to test the Prophet, so that his compliance would disprove revelation. Besides the inconsistency in that account, a serious divine proof would be needless in reply to a baseless test.

The shift from addressing them directly to speaking of “them” apparently prepares for God’s command to the Prophet. The manifest signs are self-evident proofs from God and disclose His will, including rejection of idols and what displeases Him. The Prophet’s answer to the demand for alteration is that he has neither authority nor right to change the Qurʾan, since it is revelation rather than his own speech. “I follow only what is revealed to me” explains why he cannot alter it, and his fear of punishment for disobeying his Lord explains why he follows revelation.

Their demand stems from not expecting the encounter with God, whereas the Prophet is certain of it and fears the punishment of that tremendous Day. Replacing the earlier expression of encounter with “a tremendous day” adds a warning, since punishment is especially fittingly connected with a tremendous Day.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that wa lā adrā-kum bihi means that God made the Qurʾan known to them, while ʿumur means a lifetime. The verse answers their request for another Qurʾan: its revelation is subject solely to God’s will, not to the Messenger’s choice. Had God willed a different Qurʾan, he would neither have recited this one nor informed them of it.

The Prophet had lived among them for a lifetime before revelation, and they knew that he had possessed no knowledge of Qurʾanic revelation. Had its production been his own power, he would have brought it forth earlier and its signs would have appeared before then. God’s will is attached to this Qurʾan rather than another, and the verse asks whether they do not understand this.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as a rebuke: none is a greater wrongdoer than one who fabricates a lie against God or denies His signs, for wrongdoing against God is the gravest wrongdoing. In the immediate context, the Prophet cannot grant the demand to alter or replace the Qurʾan. Altering what they reject would be fabricating lies against God; abandoning this Qurʾan for another acceptable to them would be denying His signs. The guilty do not succeed.

It is also possible that both clauses address the polytheists: their association of partners with God fabricates lies against Him, and their rejection of the Prophet’s mission and revealed verses denies His signs. A further view divides the address, applying fabrication to the Prophet if he complied and denial to the polytheists. Though not intrinsically objectionable, that reading is not readily derived from the wording; the first explanation is more suited to the context.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse is directed primarily to idolatrous polytheists, though its scope may include others such as the People of the Book. Idolaters worshipped images in order to approach the lords represented by them and, through those delegated beings, the Lord of Lords. Because of their own impurity and sins, they considered direct approach to God impossible; they therefore worshipped idols in hope that the idols or their lords would bring benefit, avert harm, and intercede with God.

The wording exposes the defect in this claim: what they worship neither harms nor benefits them. For their worship to serve its alleged end, these objects would have to perceive their devotion and possess the capacity to benefit or harm, so that intercession could occur if God accepted it. Yet idols are lifeless and have neither awareness nor such power.

“Will you inform Allah about something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?” is a rhetorical negation of the alleged intercessors’ existence. God knows all that is in heaven and earth, and intercession itself requires that the one appealed to know the intercessor and the intercession. Their claim therefore amounts to an arrogant fabrication. “Immaculate is He and exalted above any partners that they ascribe!” is God’s own declaration of transcendence, not part of the Prophet’s commanded speech, as its third-person reference to the idolaters indicates.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan distinguishes two forms of human disagreement. One concerns worldly claims and conflicts between claimants and defendants, oppressors and oppressed; God addresses it by establishing religion, sending prophets, and revealing the Book to judge disputes and teach religion. The other is disagreement within religion and its true knowledge, in the roots and branches of faith. It results from the envy of those given the Book after knowledge has come to them, opens the paths of guidance and misguidance, and is the kind of disagreement for which God has said that, but for a prior decree, He would judge between them at an appointed time.

The preceding mention of worshipping powerless beings and taking them as intercessors shows that this verse concerns the second kind. Mankind had been one community in the religion of monotheism, then divided into monotheists and polytheists. Their disagreement would call for judgment by the triumph of truth over falsehood, including the destruction of falsifiers and salvation of the truthful. The prior word delaying that judgment is God’s word when He sent mankind to earth: On the earth shall be your abode and sustenance for a time (2:36).

The commentary rejects the claim that “mankind” means only Arabs following Abraham’s religion until ʿAmr b. Luḥayy introduced idolatry, since the wording provides no linguistic evidence for this restriction. It also rejects the view that mankind have always been one community in fiṭrat al-Islām while perpetually differing in actuality: this opposes the apparent sense of the verse and verses describing division as arising from envy after knowledge, and cannot consistently make perpetual disagreement contrary to human nature.

More untenable is the view that all mankind initially followed kufr and shirk and later divided into Muslims and disbelievers. It lacks evidence and reverses the Qurʾanic sequence, in which jealousy and enmity after knowledge lead to disbelief and polytheism. It would also make the cause of humanity’s destruction innate, undermining the purpose of creation; the commentary compares this to the Christian account of atonement in which human disobedience nullifies creation’s purpose and is rectified by Christ’s sacrifice.

Finally, “a prior word” cannot mean Your Lord will indeed judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ (10:93). “Prior” concerns revelation, whereas that verse comes later in a sūrah revealed all at once, and its context specifically concerns the Israelites. The prior divine judgment must instead follow God’s first statement concerning mankind’s misguidance, associationism, and disobedience: His word upon sending them down to earth.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan treats this demand for a sign as part of the polytheists’ recurring wrongs and as connected with their earlier response to the recitation of the Qurʾan. Even if they request a sign in addition to the Qurʾan, their words express contempt for it and deny that it is a divine sign. The reply, “The Unseen belongs only to Allah,” means that signs belong to the Unseen and are exclusively God’s affair, not the Prophet’s; if the Qurʾan and its teachings do not satisfy them, they must wait, as he waits with them.

The verse also suggests that the Prophet awaited a decisive sign, besides the Qurʾan, that would distinguish truth from falsehood and judge between him and his people. What they are commanded to await is further explained by: Whether We show you a part of what We promise them, or take you away, their return will be to Us. Then Allah will be witness to what they do (10:46).
verses.21:
Al-Mizan says that, although the verse has a general application, its context concerns the polytheists’ scheming with God’s signs after they have tasted mercy following distress. The Qurʾan itself is one such sign and mercy, granted after the ignorance, hardship, humiliation, division, discord, and hatred that afflicted them. Yet they scheme against it by demanding another or altered Qurʾan and by asking why another sign has not been sent down.

Their scheming will harm them rather than benefit them, for God is swifter in devising, and their plot against His signs is itself God’s devising against them. “Taste” indicates their receiving only a small portion of divine mercy; mercy after distress (darrāʾ), rather than mere ease (sarrāʾ), shows that their relief is divine favor rather than necessarily something they deserve. They ought to acknowledge that mercy, affirm their Lord’s oneness, and give thanks. Instead, they explain away the signs, for example by treating alternating prosperity and adversity as merely the experience of their forefathers, or by offering unacceptable excuses such as ‘Should we follow the guidance with you, we will be dispossessed of our territory’ (28:57).

“Our messengers write down what you scheme” means that watchers record and preserve their deeds, so that recompense is assigned before their plot takes effect, or it does not take effect. The commentary further takes the apparent sense of This is Our book, which speaks truly against you. Indeed We used to record what you used to do (45:29) to mean that the angels bring deeds from potentiality into external reality, inscribing the acts themselves upon the page of the cosmos. Their supposed concealed plotting is thus God’s bringing their inward plots into actuality; their belief that they plot against Him and proceed in it is itself a recompense by which He misguides them for what they have earned.

The sudden shift to direct address in “what you scheme” perhaps enacts the statement that God is swifter in devising: God directly confronts them with the reason, then returns to speaking of them in the third person. The commentary considers this perhaps among the Qurʾan’s finest shifts of address.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains that fulk can be singular or plural, but here means ships, as shown by “they sail with them.” A rīḥ ʿāṣif is a fiercely blowing wind, and those who think they are besieged believe that the sea is about to engulf and destroy them. Their plea for deliverance refers to rescue from the storm’s severity.

The transition from “you are in the ships” to “they sail with them” is an eloquent shift from direct address to the third person. It perhaps indicates their return to a state of absence from God, while God turns to the Prophet to relate the most remarkable part of their story. It also hints that God ceases commanding the Prophet to address the idolaters directly because they do not understand speech.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that baghī basically means seeking, but is chiefly used for wrongdoing because it denotes seeking what belongs to another by infringing that person’s rights. The qualification bi ghayr ḥaqq, “unduly,” confirms that this is not its primary lexical meaning.

The account of people sailing, invoking God in danger, and then committing violations after rescue exemplifies the preceding statement about those who scheme against God’s signs after receiving mercy; it may specifically exemplify “Allah is more swift at devising.” Its purpose culminates in: “O mankind! Your violations are only to your own detriment.”

The shift to this direct address is God’s own speech to all mankind, not speech commanded to the Prophet, as shown by “then to Us will be your return.” Like the direct address in (10:21), it confronts people with God’s presence and complete knowledge while they suppose that He is absent from their intentions and aims. Their violations occur only by His leave and through His hands, so they cannot transgress against Him; rather, they harm themselves, are distanced from Him, and have their sins recorded. They enjoy the wares of this world only briefly, return to Him, and are informed of the reality of what they did.

According to Ḥafṣ and ʿĀṣim, “the wares of the life of this world” is accusative, meaning that they will enjoy the world’s wares. Under the nominative recitation, it is the predicate of an implied subject: their violations and deeds are nothing but the wares of this world. In either reading, the phrase explains why their violations are only to their own detriment.
verses.24: Al-Mizan says that, after mentioning worldly enjoyment, the verse gives an allegorical representation of the world’s reality for those who reflect, rather than a direct comparison. The earth’s vegetation flourishes through rain, becomes adorned with zukhruf, and seems securely possessed by its inhabitants, but God’s edict suddenly makes it like a mown field, as though it had not flourished the day before. Zukhruf means adornment and beauty; “it did not flourish” signifies that remaining in a place for a long time brings no benefit.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan explains yadʿū as inviting by drawing the invitee’s attention toward the object of invitation. It is broader than nidāʾ, which is a call made through words and sounds, whereas an invitation may be by words, gestures, or otherwise and need not be vocal.

God’s invitation is creative and legislative. Creatively, He brings into existence what He wills, as though inviting it to His will; “The day He invites you, you will respond to Him, praising Him” (17:52) means His invitation to the life of the Hereafter, to which people respond. Legislatively, He directs people through the language of His signs to what He wills in religion. The servant’s duʿāʾ is the pursuit of divine mercy and regard through a posture of servitude and submission. Worship is therefore, in reality, supplication: through humility and subordination to the Master, the servant seeks His regard. This is the reality indicated by: Your Lord has said, ‘Call Me, and I will hear you!’ Indeed those who are disdainful of My worship will enter hell in utter humility (40:60).

The author of al-Manār denies that worship is among the meanings of duʿāʾ in legislated worship, arguing that fasting, for example, is not supplication; he holds that every religious supplication is worship, but not every religious worship is supplication. Al-Mizan traces this confusion to defining supplication merely as calling for something and neglecting its deeper analysis.

According to al-Rāghib in the Mufradāt, salām originally means freedom from internal and external harm, a meaning present in its derivatives. It differs from salāma in that peace is safety in itself, while security is safety in relation to that from which one is safe. God is al-Salām because His essence is pure good without evil. Paradise is the Abode of Peace because its inhabitants suffer no evil or harm; the statement that it is so called because it is God’s abode ultimately has the same basis, since God is al-Salām by being free of evil.

The unqualified salām in the verse denotes absolute peace, which exists only in Paradise. Worldly peace is relative: every worldly thing is impeded from what it seeks and has contraries and opposites. Absolute safety from everything disliked entails possessing whatever one wishes, so the Abode of Peace corresponds to the description that there they will have whatever they wish. Its being with their Lord further shows that qurb is their ḥuḍūr with Him and their never being heedless of Him there.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains al-ḥusnā as the best reward and ziyāda as an addition beyond what the virtuous deserve. Although recompense for good is itself divine grace, God has made it due to those who do good; He then augments it, making even the addition a right for them. The increase may thus be a like reward or many times its like.

If al-ḥusnā instead means the best outcome, no further outcome can be conceived beyond it. The increase must then be a grace beyond human comprehension: Paradise contains all that people could wish for, while its further gift exceeds even their understanding.

Yarhaq means to cover or attach, and qatar is black smoke or dust. The absence of soot and abasement from the believers’ faces contrasts with the dwellers of Hell: soot is outward darkness and abasement inward darkness. Thus, those virtuous in this world receive the best reward—or outcome—together with God’s increase, remain free of these two darknesses, and abide eternally in Paradise.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan interprets the verse to mean that those who commit evil receive only a punishment proportionate to what they have earned: the requital of an evil deed is an evil outcome. They will have no protector against God’s punishment; this excludes every supposed means of repelling it, whether an associate, intercessor, powerful adversary, or anything else.

The image of qiṭaʿ min al-layl muẓlim portrays the dark night as divided into pieces, with one piece covering each idolater’s face and wholly shrouding it in darkness. It does not mean that successive pieces are layered over the face, for the wording gives no indication of this. Finally, aṣḥāb al-nār and hum fīhā khālidūn together establish that they will remain in Hell forever, just as the corresponding language in the preceding verse establishes the everlasting abode of Paradise’s inhabitants.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan states that the gathering includes believers, idolaters, and the alleged partners. The command for the idolaters and their partners to remain in their places discloses their separation: the bond between them was only illusion and false supposition. Their worship never truly reached the supposed partners, who were not partners in reality.

Accordingly, the partners’ words, “It was not us that you worshipped,” are a truthful and serious denial, attested by God’s witness and by their unawareness of the alleged worship. They do not merely mean that they did not command such worship, nor that the idolaters really worshipped only their desires or the devils that misled them. True worship is a relation of servitude and humility connected to its object, and this connection requires that the object be aware of it. Without such awareness there is only the outward form of worship, not worship in reality.

The Day therefore unveils what worldly desires and illusions had concealed: ownership, lordship, and sovereignty belong to God alone, and none besides Him has a share that could justify seeking help from it or worshipping it. The polytheists will see that their alleged partners were neither real partners nor real objects of their worship, even though their acts had the outward appearance of worship. This is the sense in which the partners’ denial is true, as indicated by their response to the polytheists’ profession, ‘Our Lord! These are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You.’ But they will retort to them, ‘You are indeed liars!’ (16:86).

The commentary rejects the view that the denial means only, “You did not worship us at our command,” since this would make the denial a morally significant lie, which cannot occur in the Hereafter. It also rejects the claim that the statement establishes worship of desires and devils instead of idols. Calling their conduct worship of desires and Satan is valid in one respect, because they followed both; yet this does not negate its being worship of idols as well. The idols deny being worshipped in order to repudiate partnership with God, not to identify another object of worship. Otherwise, their claim that they were unaware of the worship would be pointless, since desires and inanimate idols alike are unaware.

Although lying as a morally significant deed is excluded in the Hereafter, false speech arising from worldly attributes may occur, as in: Then their only excuse will be to say, ‘By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.’ Look, how they forswear themselves, and what they used to fabricate has forsaken them! (6:23–24). The partners’ particular concern is to clear themselves of alleged partnership; their asserted unawareness shows that, had they knowingly received worship, they would in some sense have borne guilt for being made partners beside God.
verses.29: Al-Mizan says that the declaration’s meaning is clear from what has already been discussed.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains tablū as “to examine,” and “there” as the station where the idolaters and their alleged partners have been set apart. At that station every soul is tested concerning what it sent ahead, and the reality of its deeds is disclosed by direct witnessing rather than merely by an account or explanation.

This direct vision reveals God as the real master and causes all illusions and fabricated claims to vanish. Such falsehoods arise from the worldly connections people posit among causes and from the independence and authority they wrongly assign to those causes. When reality is unveiled, it becomes evident that no true guardian or authority exists except God; fabricated deities are nullified, and every deed is futile except deeds in which God was truly worshipped.

The three clauses of the verse thus explain one another. Together they manifest, directly and unambiguously on the Day of Resurrection, the reality of divine guardianship: all besides God possess only neediness and servitude, while the foundations of every false claim and illusion collapse.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that rizq is continuous sustenance: provision from heaven includes rain and snow, while provision from earth includes the plants and animals through which human life continues. God’s control of hearing and sight means His sovereignty over the human senses by which people distinguish desirable from harmful things and benefit from provision. Hearing and sight are singled out because of their especially evident role in vital activity, though God grants, withholds, increases, and diminishes all the senses.

Life first appears as the principle through which knowledge, power, and actions manifest, while death ends those vital acts. Observation shows that life is not confined to animals: plants too possess the vital principle reflected in their various activities and living cells. More generally, life is whatever state enables a thing to produce its proper effects, and death is the absence of that state. Thus earth lives by greenness and flourishing; an action lives by attaining its purpose; a word lives by affecting its hearer; and human life consists in following innate guidance through sound intellect (ʿaql) and a pure soul. Religion is therefore life for humanity, since true religion, Islam, accords with the God-given nature upon which humans were originated.

Accordingly, bringing forth the living from the dead may mean the emergence of animals, or animals and plants, from sperm, eggs, and seeds, and the separation of lifeless parts from living beings. In its broader sense, it means the emergence of what is beneficial from what is not beneficial, and conversely: living humans, animals, and plants from dead soil; the wise and righteous from one lacking intellect and righteousness and vice versa; and believers from disbelievers and disbelievers from believers. The verse’s address to idolaters apparently intends this latter sense.

The idolaters held that the diverse celestial and earthly domains required separate mediators before God, whose idols they worshipped to approach the Supreme Deity. The verse overturns this premise by showing that every domain of governance ultimately depends on God. Since they themselves acknowledge that provision, human benefit, and the direction of all affairs belong to Him, He alone is the Lord and no other is worthy of lordship.

The verse proceeds from matters especially concerning people—provision—to what benefits all beings—the direction of the command. Hearing, sight, and the bringing forth of life and death accordingly concern human affairs in particular. Human life here is the possession of intellect and religion, so bringing forth living from dead means bringing forth one flourishing in human happiness from one devoid of it, and the reverse.

God thus commands the Prophet to ask who sends rain, causes growth, provides the means of sustenance, controls the senses by which people recognize beneficial provision, brings forth benefit from its opposite and the felicitous from the wretched and vice versa, and directs the whole creation. The idolaters must answer, “Allah,” for they admit that this governance returns to Him. They are therefore rebuked for worshipping other deities despite this acknowledgment and called to affirm His oneness and worship Him alone: “W ill you not then be wary?” The conclusion follows in the next verse: That, then, is Allah, your true Lord (10:32).
verses.32:
Al-Mizan holds that “That, then, is Allah, your true Lord” concludes the preceding proof: the One acknowledged to govern all things is the only true Lord. “So what is there after the truth except error?” is consequently a judgment that idol worship is misguidance. Guidance belongs with truth and worship of God alone; whoever follows falsehood has only error.

The wording concisely implies both, “What is there after truth except falsehood?” and, “What is there after guidance except error?” Some scholars describe this as reciprocal ellipsis (iḥtibāk): “falsehood” is omitted from the first clause and “guidance” from the second, each being indicated by its opposite. “Then where are you being led away?” asks how long they will turn from truth and its guidance toward the misguidance accompanying falsehood.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan takes the “word” made due against transgressors to be God’s inevitable decree that, so long as they persist in transgression, they will not believe or receive guidance to faith: and Allah does not guide the transgressing lot (5:108). “Thus” refers to the preceding conclusion that, by turning from truth, the polytheists transgressed and entered misguidance, since there is no position between truth and falsehood, or guidance and misguidance.

The divine decree that they will not believe has become established in reality because they themselves turned from truth and transgressed; it is not an arbitrary or unjust deprivation of guidance. The verse also indicates that even self-evident propositions and laws, including the absence of a middle ground between truth and falsehood, have a basis in the divine decree (al-qaḍāʾ al-ilāī), rather than being independently established in God’s realm by their own natures.

Some commentators interpret “word” as a decree of punishment, treating “that they shall not have faith” as its cause through an implicit lām. Al-Mizan finds this flawed: the relation between the conclusive argument and punishment is not apparent or agreed upon, since the argument stands inherently, whereas punishment is due for another reason, namely unbelief.

The idolaters acknowledged God as Creator and Sustainer and acknowledged that cosmic governance belongs to Him, yet diverted this truth to affirm separate lords for separate affairs and worshipped their images in hope of their intercession. The verse instead draws the consequence entailed by their own admission: true lordship belongs to God alone, and He alone deserves worship.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse argues from the origin and return—that is, Creation and Resurrection. The One who originates all things and restores them deserves worship from those who are wary of the Day of the Encounter, seeking safety from its painful punishment and attainment of its great reward. Since the addressed polytheists do not believe in the Resurrection, God commands the Prophet himself to answer: “Allah originates the creation, then He will bring it back,” and to rebuke their continued straying from truth.

This argument does not rest on an unproved premise. Divine speech establishes the Resurrection by, among other approaches, the necessity that God’s acts have an ultimate purpose and divine justice (al-ʿadl al-ilāhī), which requires recompense for deeds; the Qurʾan has refuted objections to resurrection and judgment more than ten times. The argument here is directed generally to believers who worship God from fear of punishment or hope for the Resurrection’s reward.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that yahdī ilā al-ḥaqq and yahdī li al-ḥaqq both mean “to guide to the truth.” The verb yahdī may govern its object with either ilā or li, so li in this verse does not mean “because.”

This is the third argument, a rational proof especially suited to the elect among believers. Human nature and reason make following truth unconditionally obligatory. Even one who follows error through mistake, doubt, or desire does so only because he takes it to be truth. It is therefore necessary to follow the one who guides to truth through the truth he possesses, rather than one who does not guide to truth or directs people elsewhere; following such a guide is itself following truth.

The polytheists cannot claim that their partners guide to truth. Whether lifeless idols and statues or beings such as angels, deities, jinn, and tyrants, they cannot bring harm or benefit, death, life, or resurrection even for themselves. God alone guides every being to its end and to what its existence requires. He guides human beings to the happiness of life and calls them to Paradise and forgiveness by sending messengers, revealing scriptures, legislating laws, and commanding believers to spread the true religion. Truth in belief, speech, and action is true only insofar as it conforms to the cosmic order, which is God’s action upon reality; thus truth is true through His will and desire.

Since God guides to truth and their partners neither guide nor are guided without others, reason gives priority to following Him. The comparative wording, “worthier to be followed,” does not deny that God alone must be followed and that others have no share in truth. Rather, it presents the proof as a comparison to make it easier for idolaters to accept and to avoid arousing their prejudice and foolishness.

The unusual contrast between “He who guides to the truth” and “he who is guided not unless he is guided” is significant. The latter apparently means one who can only be guided by another and cannot guide himself. Though the grammatical opposites might seem to be “guides” and “does not guide,” or “is guided” and “is not guided,” their pairing indicates that one guided by another is not guided to the truth in the requisite sense, whereas one innately guided to truth can guide others to it. Whoever truly guides to truth must himself be guided, but not through another’s guidance; one dependent on another does not bring others to the explicit truth and core of reality.

Ordinary speech loosely calls anyone who states truth or summons others to it a guide, even if he does not believe, practise, or fully understand it, or has himself been guided by another. But the guidance meant here is not mere direction to a path; it is conveying people to the intended end. It belongs only to God and to those whom He guides without an intermediary between them and Himself, who then guide by God’s command. Such guidance may be theirs from the beginning or through a special divine grace, as with prophets and their successors among the Imāms. Showing and describing the path, by contrast, is not confined to God, prophets, or Imāms.

The clause “or he who is guided not, except that he be guided” includes everyone who does not guide himself: both those who can be guided by another and those incapable of guidance, such as idols. Its verbal construction, an yuhdā, does not assert that guidance has actually occurred; it denotes the need to be guided. Whoever can receive guidance may be guided by another, whereas one unable to receive it remains unguided.

Al-Mizan rejects several proposed readings. To make the exception exhaustive, so that anyone may guide after God guides him, distorts the verse’s point: one not personally guided to truth cannot lead others to it. It also fails to include idols, the primary object of the argument, while shifting attention to figures such as Jesus, Ezra, and angels. To treat the exception as discontinuous and restrict “he who is guided not” to idols makes the comparison fail unless extra words are supplied, and arbitrarily excludes other unguided beings. To read illā as “until” makes the qualification superfluous and lacks a sound basis in classical Arabic, apart from rare and ineloquent alleged instances. To refer the clause to angels, jinn, or misguided leaders likewise removes it from the immediate debate with idol worshippers.

God is the inherent and true possessor of guidance; others can possess such a function only subordinately, through His bestowal and by His leave, just as with other divine functions. Thus prophets and Imāms may guide by His command, and the narrations state that guiding humankind to truth is the responsibility of the Prophet and his Household. The closing question, “What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”, expresses astonishment at following partners who neither are guided nor guide to truth, contrary to reason’s plain judgment.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan notes that yughnī may take either min or ʿan, both usages occurring in the Qurʾan. The verse attributes conjecture to most disbelievers because only a minority—the leaders of error—know the truth but prefer falsehood out of enmity and call others to it. The majority blindly follow these leaders’ opinions because they think well of them.

“Indeed Allah knows best what they do” grounds the statement about their conjecture: God fully knows that they are following conjecture, and conjecture is no substitute for the truth (lā yughnī min al-ḥaqq shayʾan).
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that mā kāna negates not merely the occurrence of fabrication but its very possibility: the Qurʾan is by its nature incapable of having been fabricated and falsely ascribed to Allah by anyone else. This construction is therefore more emphatic than simply saying that fabrication did not occur.

Its confirmation of what was before it (bayna yadayhi) means its confirmation of the already present revealed scriptures, specifically the Torah and the Evangel. Although all earlier scriptures preceded the Qurʾan, this expression—literally “between its hands”—denotes those closest to it and extant at its time, not merely previously revealed doctrines such as the Resurrection or Recompense.

The Book means divine scripture sent down to the prophets, and tafṣīl is the clarification and separation of matters previously combined or summarized. The verse thus indicates that the religions divinely revealed to the prophets are one, differing only in their degree of detail: the Qurʾan elaborates what earlier scriptures summarized and is guardian over them, as indicated in (3:19) and (5:48). “There is no doubt in it” follows from its being from the Lord of all the worlds; its divine source explains its freedom from doubt.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan takes “or” to introduce the assertion that the Prophet fabricated the Qurʾan. The response challenges its proponents: if it were fabricated human discourse, they should bring a chapter like it, summoning any helpers besides Allah. Calling a chapter “like” the Qurʾan also shows that “Qurʾan” may designate either a large or small portion of the scripture.

The challenge is to produce something like any chapter, long or short, and is not confined to a particular type of chapter, to narratives and predictions rather than commands, or to a long chapter containing fundamental teachings. Since the whole Qurʾan is ascribed to God, calling any part fabricated implicates the whole; there is no relevant distinction between statements and commandments, long and short chapters, or even a chapter and a single verse.

Its inimitability is not confined to eloquence and rhetorical power. It rests on the Qurʾan’s comprehensive perfection: its divine teachings and religious laws; moral and social guidance; accounts of prophets and past nations; knowledge of the Unseen and future prophecies; descriptions of angels, jinn, heaven, earth, and the Origin and Return; wisdom, exhortation, promises and warnings; cogent arguments, illumination, guidance, and the harmony of all its parts—together with an eloquence beyond human reach.

Al-Mizan criticizes early scholars who reduced its miracle to verbal eloquence, thereby neglecting its truths and knowledge and treating its meanings as equally available to everyone. God instead characterizes it as light, mercy, guidance, wisdom, admonition, clear proof, a clarification of all things, a detailed book, healing for believers, and a decisive, non-jesting statement, as having no discrepancy within it; He does not explicitly characterize it by eloquence. The declaration that neither people nor jinn, even united and assisted by others, can produce its like is likewise unrestricted to eloquence alone.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that their charge of fabrication arises from denying what they do not comprehend in the Qurʾan: its genuine wisdom and actual sciences exceed their grasp, while the fulfilment (taʾwīl) of what they deny has not yet reached them. When that fulfilment comes, they will have no choice but certainty and belief.

The context directs taʾwīl to the Day of Resurrection, as (7:53) indicates. In Qurʾanic usage, taʾwīl is the reality on which an idea depends—whether a commandment, teaching, story, or another matter—rather than a component of the idea’s verbal meaning. The whole Qurʾan, including its teachings, ordinances, and reports, has such a taʾwīl. It is therefore not merely the explanation of Qurʾanic words.

The comparison with earlier deniers confirms this reading: previous polytheists likewise rejected their prophets’ teachings and rulings because they did not comprehend them and had not yet encountered their fulfilment. The present deniers are the same. Their ignorance keeps them from certainty until the Resurrection, when the veils over divine realities are lifted, the truth of religion becomes manifest, and the fate of former wrongdoers foreshadows their own.
verses.40: Al-Mizan says that the verse divides people into those who believe in the Qurʾan and those who do not. By calling the latter mufsidīn, it indicates that their denial of its teachings arises from moral corruption. It rejects the view that the verse instead predicts that the Prophet’s people will divide into permanent believers and unbelievers, unlike earlier peoples who were eradicated, since this reading is unsupported by the wording.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded, when they deny him, to disassociate himself from them: his deeds are his responsibility and theirs are theirs, so each is absolved of the other’s acts. Such tabarrī is a stage of supporting the truth (al-intiṣār li al-ḥaqq): one first guides those willing to be guided, then disassociates from those who refuse, lest they pressure one into following their falsehood.
verses.42: Al-Mizan reads the question as a denial: although some listen to the Prophet, he cannot make the deaf hear when they do not apply reason. Their deafness is that of the heart; because they do not grasp the significance of what they hear, they are as though physically deaf.
verses.43: Al-Mizan says that this verse has the same meaning as the preceding one: some observe the Prophet, yet he cannot guide those who are blind when they do not perceive.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains that their deprivation of hearing and sight, expressed as deafness and blindness, results from their own wrongdoing. Allah has not wronged them by taking these capacities away; they have brought this condition upon themselves.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan reads the verse to mean that, on the day Allah gathers them, those who denied the encounter with Him will be seen to have lost. They will regard their worldly stay as no more than an hour of a day and will recognize one another without denying or forgetting one another. Grammatically, “the day” qualifies their loss, “as if they had not remained except for an hour” qualifies them, and “getting acquainted with one another” further qualifies that brief remaining. Alternative readings that make these phrases adjectival in other ways are not supported by the wording.

The verse returns to the encounter with God and to the fulfilment (taʾwīl) of religious prophecy. Though that fulfilment has not yet come, people must not be deceived by the seemingly fixed, lengthy life of this world. When they are mustered before God, its brevity will be plain; the fulfilment of religion will disclose the truth, monotheism will become manifest, and it will be clear that the Day belongs to God, the One, the All-paramount.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains that whether God shows the Prophet part of the promised punishment or takes him before it occurs, the deniers will in every case return to God. “Then” marks a logical order, not a temporal sequence, since God is always witness to their deeds. The verse consoles the Prophet, introduces the coming discussion of punishment, and assures him that the deeds calling it down are neither hidden from God nor forgotten. The shift from direct address—“We show you”—to “Allah will be witness” draws attention to God’s all-encompassing witnessing, proper to His utter divinity.
verses.47: Al-Mizan holds that the verse expresses two divine decrees: every nation receives a messenger who conveys God’s message, and, after the people divide into believers and deniers, God judges between them justly and without wronging them. The concise phrase “when their messenger comes” implicitly includes his delivery of the message and their disagreement over it; judgment, especially concerning punishment and harm, presupposes such a dispute. This judgment belongs specifically to divine messengership, rasūl, rather than prophecy, nabī.
verses.48: Al-Mizan interprets the question as being asked by idolaters contemporary with the Prophet about the time of the promised worldly judgment between them. Their being directed to the answer, “I have no control over any benefit for myself nor any harm except what Allah may wish. There is a time for every nation …” (10:49), supports this reading. The view that it concerns Resurrection punishment and idolaters of earlier nations is rejected.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters impatiently demand to know when God will fulfill His promise to judge between them and the Prophet, destroy them, save the believers, and free the latter from their evil. Their demand is a challenge and mockery. The Prophet is first commanded to declare that he cannot bring benefit or repel harm even from himself, except as God wills; therefore he cannot hasten the promised judgment, which lies wholly with God.

The answer does not specify its time, because that belongs to the Unseen and to God’s exclusive command: “The Unseen belongs only to Allah. So wait. I too am waiting along with you” (10:20). Instead, it establishes its inevitability through the universal norm that every nation has an appointed term which it can neither postpone nor advance. The Prophet’s community is likewise a nation with such a term.

A nation consequently has a collective life beyond its members’ individual lives: an ordained existence and duration, and its own portion of happiness and misery, obligations, guidance and misguidance, reward and punishment. Divine governance attends to nations as it attends to individuals. History, ruined dwellings, and the Qurʾanic accounts of Noah’s people, ʿAḍ, Thamūd, Abraham’s people, Lot’s people, Pharaoh’s people, and others attest that nations perished through divine punishment only after their messengers brought clear proofs and their people divided between belief and denial, the deniers being the majority.

Thus the Prophet’s audience, having divided over the truth brought to them, will also be judged between their messenger and themselves and may be seized as earlier nations were. Though the threat begins with the polytheists, it also reaches wrongdoers among the Muslims. They must not imagine that their community is exempt from worldly punishment as an honor to the Prophet, or that sin and transgression are safe because of such an honor; honor with God comes only through piety. “It will be neither after your hopes nor the hopes of the People of the Book: whoever commits evil shall be requited for it, and he will not find for himself any guardian or helper besides Allah” (4:123).

The belief that both worldly and otherworldly punishment are forgiven for this community, leaving people free to act as they please while assured of forgiveness and Paradise, would make religion and divine law arbitrary rules and falsely attribute such play to God. Al-Mizan traces this delusion to turning away from God’s remembrance and neglecting His Book: “And the Messenger will say, ‘O my Lord! Indeed my people consigned this Qurʾan to oblivion.’” (25:30)
verses.50:
Al-Mizan notes that bayātan means “by night,” like laylan, but is especially used of harm such as an enemy attack. The idolaters’ question about when the promise will be fulfilled shows that they seek to hasten the divine punishment which would compel belief.

After establishing its inevitability, the verses rebuke them in two respects. First, they seek to hasten a sudden punishment, whether by night or day, which guilty people should fear and cannot escape. The shift from directly addressing them to referring to “the guilty” both reflects that they have not explicitly spoken evil and indicates that their guilt is why punishment comes upon them. Second, they defer belief until punishment arrives, when it no longer benefits them: destruction would force belief, but belief is a form of repentance, and repentance is not accepted once punishment’s signs appear and death is imminent. “Now?” reproaches them for believing only at the moment they had mockingly and heedlessly urged to come.

verses.52: Al-Mizan considers the verse apparently connected to “There is a time for every nation” (10:48), with (10:50-51) functioning as an interjection. The former establishes the certainty of the wrongdoers’ worldly punishment and destruction; afterward they are told to taste the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter, recompense only for their earned deeds and sins. The command is a figurative expression for punishment’s encompassing and reaching them.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains that “it” refers, according to the context, either to God’s judgment or to the divine punishment, whose significance here is the same. The Prophet is commanded to affirm from every angle that it will inevitably occur and cannot be obstructed. “Yes! By my Lord, it is indeed true (innahu la-ḥaqun)” intensifies this assurance through the oath and through inna and the lām of emphasis.
verses.54: Al-Mizan says that the verse emphasizes punishment’s severity and the need for wrongdoers to escape it: were they to own all that is on earth, they would offer it as ransom. They will feel remorse on seeing the punishment, but conceal it, apparently from fear of ridicule or a similar reason. The apparent sense is that the decree and punishment in view are worldly, not the punishment of the Hereafter; judgment is nevertheless rendered between them justly and without wrong.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan presents the verse and what follows as a rational proof that the promised punishment is true, inevitable, and incapable of being prevented. Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God alone; hence all disposal belongs solely to Him, and no one has any control except by His permission. His action depends only on His will, not on external requirements, assistance, or impediments. What He wills occurs, and His promise cannot be altered by any external factor.

Most people fail to grasp this because they compare God’s dominion with that of powerful human rulers. A ruler may seem absolute, yet his aims and promises depend on interests and external causes; time, changing public belief, and realities such as life, death, health, and illness lie beyond his control. His authority is ultimately dependent on people’s recognition and on causes that may or may not assist him.

God’s dominion, by contrast, means that every thing’s existence depends on Him, is created and disposed by His command, and is subject to His will. Whatever control exists is His alone and occurs only by His leave, so nothing can depart from His will or be attributed independently to another. His acts necessarily disclose His intent. Falsehood and error concern mental concepts in their relation to external reality, whereas God’s promise is His future act, unseen to us, for which He has directed all causes; there can be no reversal.

Reflection on this sovereignty shows why Allah’s promise is necessarily true, and doubt arises only from ignorance of His exalted position. The verse therefore states God’s ownership of all things as the premise and the truth of His promise as its conclusion, adding that most do not know. The following verse further expounds this dominion through God’s giving life and bringing death.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that this completes the preceding argument from God’s dominion with respect to human beings: life, death, and return all lie under His control, so humanity cannot stand outside His dominion.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that the Qurʾan comes to all mankind from their Lord as mawʿiẓa, a heart-softening admonition that deters through warning; as a cure for what is in the breasts; as guidance; and as mercy specifically for the faithful. Since the breast is regarded as the repository of the heart’s inward qualities, its cure figuratively means the removal of spiritual vices, distress, and moral diseases that deprive a person of felicity in this world and the next. Guidance is kindly directing someone to the desired end.

Mercy, when ascribed to God, does not mean a human feeling of compassion but its effect: His bestowal of existence, sustenance, and gifts. In relation to believers, it comprises true knowledge, noble character, righteous deeds, the good life in both abodes, Paradise, and His satisfaction (riḍwān). Thus, the Qurʾan is mercy for those who understand its realities and follow its teaching.

The four descriptions set out the Qurʾan’s ordered effect on believers. It first awakens people from heedlessness, doubt, and evil habits; then purifies their souls and heals the afflictions of mind and heart; then guides them gradually to true knowledge, virtuous character, and righteous action, drawing them near to the ranks of al-muqarrabūn; and finally clothes them in mercy, honor, and the company of prophets, truthful ones, witnesses, and the righteous. It performs these functions by its own essence, as the direct connection between God and creation, not through something external to it.

The address, “O mankind!”, shows that the verse is universal, even if its surrounding discourse addresses idolaters. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that its “mercy” means merely the mutual affection shown by believers, since this conflicts with the verse’s context.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains faḍl as an excess or gift, which, when attributed to God, indicates His bounty and freedom from needing either what He gives or those to whom He gives. It is not far-fetched that “grace” denotes God’s general gifts to creation, while “mercy” denotes His particular blessings for the faithful; together, worldly provision and religious felicity are especially worthy of rejoicing. The repeated bi in “In Allah’s grace and in His mercy” indicates that each is an independent cause, while “let them rejoice in that” joins them together.

Another possible reading is that faḍl denotes the preceding blessings of admonition, cure, and guidance, while mercy is the special divine gift that gives believers a good life in this world and the Hereafter. On this reading, these religious gifts deserve greater joy than accumulated worldly wealth. Al-Mizan considers it far removed to take the grace connected with purification as merely general blessing, and says that the latter interpretation accords with narrations that interpret the verse in relation to the Prophet, ʿAlī, or the Qurʾan.

The phrase “in that” refers to God’s grace and mercy and is placed before the command in order to restrict rejoicing to them. They are better than worldly possessions because happiness in both abodes depends on them, whereas amassed wealth is only a trial and may lead to ruin and misery.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that rizq comprises the earthly things that sustain life, and that its being “sent down” signifies its descent from God’s treasuries according to His determined measure, not simply its dependence on rainfall. The provision at issue is cattle and similar animals to which the idolaters assigned religious statuses, such as waṣīla, sāʾiba, and ḥām.

The phrase la-kum means that this provision was sent down for human benefit. Since God sent it as sustenance, the wording implies that He made it lawful; the idolaters then divided it on their own into unlawful and lawful portions. The rhetorical question therefore rebukes them: they have no revelation or messenger establishing God’s sanction, so their religious rulings are fabrications against Him.

Although it might seem that such classifications could arise from perceived benefit, custom, or desire without being attributed to God, the commentary holds that the right to legislate and judge belongs to God alone. Divine judgment accords with creation and humankind’s innate disposition: God created things purposively, equipped them with the means to attain their perfection, and guided them toward it. Religion, as the laws governing acquired qualities and deeds, must therefore accord with that created nature and its goal.

Human beings’ natural equipment for nourishment, procreation, social cooperation, and other activities itself calls for the religion of innate disposition, dīn al-fiṭra. The interconnected cosmic order conveys God’s will and contains the natural law of humanity, al-sharīʿa al-fiṭriyya al-insāniyya, directing people to the true religion. Thus true religion is God’s judgment, and every judgment besides His is false and leads to misery and destruction. Every rule among people is consequently either a true divine judgment received through revelation or divine message, or a false ruling attributed to God; there is no third category. The polytheists did in fact attribute their own invented rules to Him.
verses.60: Al-Mizan states that the preceding question has already established that they fabricated lies against God; this verse therefore warns them of the grave consequences of that sin on the Day of Resurrection. God’s faḍl here is His provision to mankind, and declaring portions of it unlawful manifests ingratitude for His gifts. Their fabrication against God is itself another form of such thanklessness: they spurn His grace and will confront the reality of their deeds when they return to Him.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains shaʾn as an important beneficial matter or state, and ifāḍa as being wholly absorbed in an activity. In “neither do you recite anything from Him of the Qurʾan,” min-hu apparently refers to God: the Qurʾan recited by the Prophet originates from Him and has been sent down by Him.

The verse shifts its address: it first speaks to the Prophet in the singular, then includes him, the polytheists, and all others in the plural concerning every deed, before returning to the singular in “your Lord.” This inclusive shift, together with the plural “Our,” indicates the abundance of God’s witnesses among angels and people, all of whom He encompasses. Its purpose is to establish that God witnesses and knows every creature’s act—whether prophet, believer, or idolater—and that no one should suppose an act will escape His knowledge or reckoning on the Day of Resurrection.

The separate mention of Qurʾanic recitation emphasizes its special importance and God’s particular concern for it. It also confirms that what the Prophet recites is divine revelation, immune from alteration or falsehood both in receiving it and conveying it, since it is always “from Him.” Nothing, even an atom’s weight or anything smaller or greater, is absent, distant, or hidden from God; all things are ever present to Him and preserved in an unfading record.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan treats this as a new statement serving the chapter’s call to faith in the Book and to God’s oneness. Wilāya originally denotes the removal of every barrier between two things, and thus signifies closeness in relation, place, rank, or friendship. A walī may describe either party in a reciprocal relation of special care: God is the ally of the believing servant through guidance, commands and prohibitions, support in both abodes, Paradise, and His pleasure; the true believer is God’s ally through obedience and reception of these spiritual gifts.

Yet the verse does not include every believer among these allies. “Those who have faith, and were Godwary” indicates, through the completed faith and continuous prior Godwariness, a rank of faith beyond initial belief. Initial Islam is outward utterance of the testimonies and submission; initial faith is their general inward acceptance, which may coexist with aspects of shirk. The faith meant here is most likely complete faith, or something near it: submission refined until it encompasses every affair, accepts the full implications of God’s divinity and authority, and neither resents His command nor objects to His will. It rests on abiding certainty and perfects servanthood.

Their lack of fear and grief likewise shows this higher rank. Fear concerns anticipated harm and grief the loss of what one regards as one’s own; but those who see all dominion as God’s alone, without partner, do not claim authority even over themselves. Thus they fear and grieve over nothing in this world or the Hereafter except what God wills: they fear their Lord and may grieve over missing His honor through failure, which itself belongs to submission.

Al-Mizan rejects both the restriction of the verse to death or Resurrection and the claim that it means only freedom from the fears and griefs suffered by disbelievers. These limitations disregard the unrestricted wording and the special rank indicated by continuous Godwariness. The claim that fear and grief are inescapable human traits also measures God’s elect by ordinary people and ignores real spiritual stations. Complete monotheism means that no being acts independently of God or possesses independent dominion; one who realizes it loves, hates, fears, and grieves only for God’s sake. Other verses that describe believers without fear or grief in a particular setting do not negate this more general description.

This does not mean that good and evil, benefit and harm, ease and hardship, pleasure and pain, or blessing and affliction become indistinguishable to God’s allies. Rather, they recognize these things while denying that any power belongs to other than God. They fear only Him, or what He wills them to fear or grieve over.
