verses.64: Al-Mizan explains that the verse gives God’s allies general glad tidings to comfort and reassure them. If it announces the good news itself, what they are promised will occur in both this world and the Hereafter. If it instead means that God will give them good news in both, the verse does not specify whether the promised thing itself will occur in both abodes or only in the Hereafter. The Qurʾan’s many promises to believers also include these allies. “There is no altering the words of Allah” confirms that this glad tiding belongs to an unalterable, irrevocable decree.
verses.65: Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet over the idolaters’ attacks on his Lord and religion and their pride in idols. He was apparently grieved for God’s sake, so God reminds him that all might belongs to Him, rendering their pretensions to honor worthless, and that He hears their words and knows their condition. Were He to will, He could punish them at any time; His postponement of punishment is for the interest of the divine mission and the best outcome for the faithful. “All might belongs to Allah” and “He is the All-hearing, the All-knowing” are therefore two distinct reasons not to grieve.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that God’s ownership of all who are in the heavens and earth establishes His exclusive Lordship, for lordship is ownership together with management of what one owns. The alleged partners have no share in this ownership except in their followers’ imaginations; associating them with God rests on conjecture and delusion, not reality. The use of “whoever,” rather than “whatever,” is said by some scholars to suit the verse’s concern with sentient beings, including angels, humans, and jinn.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that this verse completes the proof of God’s Lordship. The preceding verse established His ownership, while this one establishes His management of the general affairs that preserve human livelihood and existence. Night provides rest, restoration after daytime fatigue, family comfort, enjoyment of one’s earnings, and time for worship; daylight gives visibility and prompts people toward activity, livelihood, and seeking. Human life requires both activity and rest, and their ordered alternation is a sign for those who listen.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains that having a child, in the ordinary sense, entails bodily separation, reproduction, and nurture, and is often sought as support in need. All of this is impossible for God, who is exalted above parts, gradation in action, resemblance to creatures, and every need.

The present verse argues particularly from the final point: one seeks a child for reliance when one is needy or incomplete, whereas God is the All-sufficient and owns everything in the heavens and earth. “You have no authority for this” means that they possess no proof at all for their claim. Rational evidence is instead contrary to it, since children are sought by the needy and deficient, while God is absolutely self-sufficient. The final question rebukes them for ignorantly attributing to the Lord of the Worlds what they do not know.
verses.69: Al-Mizan describes this as a warning that those who fabricate lies against God will suffer terrible consequences and will not attain felicity. The wording moves from relating their claim in the third person, to directly rebuking them for asserting without knowledge that God has taken a son, and then to speaking of fabrication “against Allah” rather than “against Me” or “against Us.” This preserves divine dignity and distances God from their ignorance. He then turns to His Messenger with the command to warn them, which belongs to the Prophet’s mission.
verses.70: Al-Mizan explains that their failure to attain felicity is due to their disbelief: they receive only a brief enjoyment in this world, then return to God and taste severe punishment for their defiance.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains Noah’s words as a challenge issued while he stood alone before his people, yet relied wholly on Allah’s protection. Maqāmī may mean either his undertaking of the prophetic mission of calling to God’s oneness or his rank as a prophet. Since his reminder of Allah’s signs had made them wish to kill or harm him, he entrusted his affair to Allah rather than managing it himself.

His command that they ajmaʿū amrakum calls on them, together with their alleged partners who they claim aid them in hardship, to unite their deliberation and resolve upon whatever course they choose. That no plan be ghumma means that nothing should remain obscured or neglected: they should exert every effort to overcome him. Their command to aqḍū ʿalayya means to finish him off, by killing or utterly destroying him, without delay. Thus Noah challenges them to act with all their combined power and their idols’ assistance, exposing their impotence and demonstrating that his Lord can protect him.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s statement follows from his trust in Allah: his people’s refusal to answer his call cannot harm him, because he has sought no reward from them that their turning away could deprive him of; his reward is solely with Allah. Being among those who submit means surrendering one’s affairs to whatever Allah wills from and for one, without arrogantly resisting His command for the worldly benefits one hopes for or the harms one fears.
verses.73: Al-Mizan explains khalāʾif as the plural of khalīfa: Allah saved Noah and those with him in the ark, made them successors on the earth, and caused later people to succeed them in their place, while drowning those who denied His signs.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan identifies these messengers as those sent after Noah until Moses. Their manifest proofs (bayyinat) were the miraculous signs their peoples demanded after the messengers had called them to the truth and been denied; these signs also included God’s judgment between the messengers and their nations. The commentary first understands the verse to say that, because of their transgression, God sealed the peoples’ hearts, so that they could not believe what they had already denied.

Their earlier denial occurred before the demanded miracles: the messengers had proclaimed God’s oneness, but the people rejected both the message and the messengers; even after receiving the requested sign, they still did not believe. Al-Mizan had also argued, in commenting on (7:101), that the prior denial refers to events in the pre-existent world (ʿālam al-dharr); it states that this does not contradict the present explanation.
verses.75: Al-Mizan explains that, after Noah and the messengers following him, God sent Moses and his brother Aaron with His signs to Pharaoh and the Egyptian elite. They arrogantly rejected those signs and persisted in their crimes.
verses.76: Al-Mizan takes “the truth” to mean God’s true signs, such as Moses’ staff becoming a serpent and his glowing hand. Though these signs attested his true message, Pharaoh’s people derided the very signs called “the truth” as plain magic.
verses.77: Al-Mizan explains that Moses rebuked their calling the truth magic through two questions: “Do you say of the truth when it comes to you” that it is magic, and “Is this magic?” The statement omitted in the first question is supplied by the second. “Magicians do not find salvation” may either explain this rebuke or independently declare that Moses disavows magic as one divinely saved, while magicians receive no salvation.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains that li-talfitanā, from laft, means to turn or divert someone away. Pharaoh and his chiefs accused Moses and Aaron of seeking to divert them from their inherited way in order to acquire supremacy—leadership, rule, and effective power—in the land. They portrayed the prophetic call as a fabricated scheme to abolish the established Pharaonic order and replace it with an Israelite state led by the two brothers; therefore, they refused belief that would enable this aim.
verses.79: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh ordered his elite to summon every expert magician to confront Moses’ miracle with magic.
verses.80: Al-Mizan explains that, when the magicians came to confront Moses, he told them to cast down what they had prepared: ropes and staffs that their magic would make appear as snakes and serpents.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ declaration would be confirmed when God made his staff into a serpent that swallowed the ropes and staffs the magicians had made to appear as serpents. What they produced was magic: it presents to the senses as real what is false in itself.

God will therefore bring it to naught, for the divine order establishes truth and defeats falsehood, even when falsehood temporarily prevails. Moses’ statement that Allah does not foster the efforts of those who cause corruption explains this: righteousness accords with the realities of the cosmic order and is enabled to endure, whereas corruption conflicts with that order. The causes and effects within the cosmos consequently oppose corruption, restoring it if possible and otherwise nullifying and erasing it; to make corruption prosper would itself corrupt the cosmic order.

Thus magic and every other falsehood cannot last. The verse expresses negatively the truth affirmed positively in the following verse: Allah confirms the truth with His words.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that “Allah will confirm the truth with His words” positively states what the preceding verse states negatively: God does not foster corrupt effort. It seems most likely that His “words” are the various divine decrees governing cosmic affairs according to truth. Since God’s decrees come to pass, falsehood cannot endure but vanishes, while truth remains.

Moses announced this reality to awaken the magicians to the divine order and prepare them for the miracle’s overwhelming triumph over magic; when they witnessed it, they hastened to faith and prostrated. The guilty detest truth’s victory because ijrām suggests severance from the path of truth: having built their lives upon that severance, its defeat entails the collapse of what they have built.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan rejects the various unsupported proposals that “his people” refers to Pharaoh—whether the believers were Egyptians, persons of mixed Israelite and Egyptian parentage, or particular members of Pharaoh’s household—or that it refers to Israelites identified as magicians, a total of 600,000 weak persons, or a surviving generation of Israelites. Nothing in the verse’s wording establishes these readings.

Its apparent meaning is that “his people” refers to Moses and that those who believed were weak members of the Children of Israel, excluding their powerful, noble elite. Since the Israelites were enslaved and ruled by Egypt, their elite sought to preserve their rank and national standing by accommodating the oppressor, and could not openly profess faith in Moses. Qurʾanic accounts further show that many of their arrogant and powerful people did not truly believe in Moses even to the end, though they outwardly obeyed measures that served Israel’s freedom and their own interests. Such obedience differed from faith in God and adherence to Moses’ teaching.

“Their elite” may therefore refer to the elites of these believing youths, who perhaps restrained them through their own disbelief or a feigned disbelief intended to please Pharaoh and avoid persecution. Pharaoh’s tyranny also gave the believers proper reason to fear torture and coercion back to his religion. If “his people” can instead encompass all who received Moses’ message among Egyptians and Israelites, the verse stands without these further explanations.

Moses’ command to trust Allah rests on faith’s knowledge that God is the ultimate cause and director of all affairs. This knowledge calls believers to submit, abandon reliance on merely apparent material causes, and entrust affairs to Him. Faith is treated as already established, while submission is its completion and a goal believers ought to attain. Thus the meaning is: since you have believed, and should submit to God, place your trust in Him.

verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that the believers entrusted themselves to God for deliverance from Pharaoh and his elite. Their prayer not to be made a test for the wrongdoing lot asks God to remove their weakness and humiliation and thereby save them from the faithless.

The weak person’s visible weakness tempts the strong oppressor to persecution, just as wealth and children can be a trial. Asking not to be such a trial therefore means asking that the cause which incites wrongdoers to mistreat them be removed. Their further plea is for deliverance, by God’s mercy, from the faithless lot.
verses.86:

The weak person’s visible weakness tempts the strong oppressor to persecution, just as wealth and children can be a trial. Their further plea is for deliverance, by God’s mercy, from the faithless lot.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains that tabawwaʾā means to take up a dwelling, and miṣr here denotes Pharaoh’s land. Moses and Aaron were commanded to establish dwellings for their people there and to arrange their houses facing one another, in one direction. This would facilitate communication, consultation, and gathering for congregational prayer, as indicated by the immediate command to maintain prayer. The wording suggests that they may previously have lived as a nomadic people, in tents or the like.

The command to give good news to the faithful concerns the fulfilment of their prayer not to be made a test for wrongdoers: God would save them from Pharaoh and his people.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains zīna as the attractive outward aspect of a thing, distinct from wealth though they may overlap; here it denotes adornments apart from their monetary value, such as jewelry, clothing, furnishings, and luxurious buildings.

The lām in li-yuḍillū cannot be purposive in the sense of an initial divine leading astray, since God neither commands error through His messengers nor wills such misguidance. It may rightly be understood as a consequence only in that primary sense. But God can lead astray as punishment and recompense for evil. Since Pharaoh and his elite obstinately persisted in arrogance and corruption, their adornment and wealth could be a recompense by which they led followers astray. Readings that make the lām a supplication or imply a negation are unsupported by the context.

To blot out their wealth is to make it decline and pass away. To harden their hearts, from shadd, is to bind and seal them so that they do not open to the truth or believe until they behold the painful punishment, when faith no longer benefits them. Interpretations that take this as keeping them in Egypt after their wealth’s destruction, or as an allusion to death and destruction, are far-fetched.

Moses made this prayer only after despairing of their faith and knowing with certainty that they would persist in error and mislead others. He asked that their worldly benefits become punishment and their hearts be sealed until the punishment overtook them. Like Noah’s prayer against his people, this was not conjecture: prophets do not speak speculatively before the Lord of the Worlds, and thus knew their people would not be guided.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains that God addresses both Moses and Aaron although Moses alone voiced the preceding supplication. This supports the reported view that Moses supplicated while Aaron affirmed it with “Amen,” so that they supplicated together.

Their prayer for Pharaoh’s painful punishment, the obliteration of his wealth, and the sealing of his heart had been granted. They were commanded to remain steadfast in calling to God and reviving the word of truth, and not to follow the way of the ignorant among the Children of Israel by yielding to demands born of desire, including demands to restore tribal and pre-Islamic custom. The answer promises Pharaoh’s punishment and his being denied success in faith, whose fulfilment the next verse details.

Neither their prayer nor its acceptance specifies whether punishment would be immediate or delayed. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports from Ibn Jurayj that Pharaoh lived another forty years after this supplication; the note attributes the report to Abū ʿAbd Allāh (al-Ṣādiq).
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh and his troops pursued the Children of Israel wrongly and tyrannically: itbāʿ is pursuit in an effort to catch, while idrāk is catching and gaining power over something. As drowning overtook him, Pharaoh professed belief in the one God in whom the Children of Israel believed—that is, God’s oneness—and claimed submission.

He described God in this way because he sought to obtain through their faith what they had obtained: passage through the sea and safety from drowning. By professing both faith and submission, he tried to remove the effects of his persistent disobedience, namely idolatry and arrogance toward God.
verses.91: Al-Mizan explains Āl-ān as contracted from the interrogative a and al-ān: “What! Now?” Pharaoh’s belief came only after punishment had overtaken him, when faith and repentance no longer avail amid death and punishment. He had spent his earlier life in disobedience and corruption without repenting in time. This fulfils Moses and Aaron’s request that he be overtaken by painful punishment and prevented from a faith that could benefit him.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan holds that God’s promise to deliver Pharaoh “through your body” indicates that Pharaoh himself was not identical with his body. What he lost when punishment overtook the body was the soul (nafs), also called the spirit (rūḥ), which God receives at death. The soul is the “I” that perceives, intends, and acts through the body, while the body is its instrument in the physical world.

Though the body is called by the person’s name because of its union with the soul, personal names truly belong to souls. The body continually changes and its parts are replaced; if personal identity belonged to the body alone, a person at old age would not be the person who acted in youth, and could not be rewarded or punished for those acts. Thus the verse is explicit, or nearly so, that souls exist beyond bodies and that bodily predicates are assigned to persons only through the soul-body union.

Accordingly, “We shall deliver you through your body” means that God would remove and save Pharaoh’s body from suffering so that it might be a sign for those after him. This is a limited deliverance attributable to Pharaoh because of that union, not preservation of his life and health in body and soul.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that deliver must derive from najwa, “high land,” on the ground that Pharaoh had died: even if his body were put on elevated ground, that body would still not be Pharaoh himself except through the same apparent union of person and body. It likewise rejects identifying badan with Pharaoh’s golden armor, or treating the expression as derision. The wording is nunajjī-ka bi-badanik, not simply “We shall deliver you”: the bi presents the body as cause or instrument and points to the union in question.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan explains that a thing attributed to truth possesses fully and genuinely what its meaning promises, without falsehood in its outcome; a true promise, for example, is one its giver will fulfil. A “true settlement” therefore provides the complete goods sought in a dwelling: good water and air, the earth’s blessings and abundance, and stable residence.

This settlement is Jerusalem and the Levant, the Holy Land in which God settled the Children of Israel. The suggestion that it was Egypt lacks Qurʾanic support; even if they later entered Egypt, they did not settle there permanently, and it does not fit the meaning of a true settlement.

The verse is a complaint and reproach. After long deprivation under Egyptian oppression, God completed His blessings, gathered and unified the Children of Israel, settled them in a true abode, and provided good things. Yet they showed ingratitude, shattered their unity, and differed over the truth not from ignorance but after knowledge had come to them. Their Lord will judge their disagreements on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.94:
Al-Mizan explains shakk as suspicion and takes “what We have sent down to you” to mean the teachings concerning creation, the Resurrection, and God’s established way of dealing with nations: messengers call them to truth, then God judges between believers and deniers. In “ask those who read the Book before you,” yaqraʾūn denotes their continuing reading, while “before you” qualifies the Book as that revealed before the Prophet.

The verse thus tells the Prophet that, if there were any misgiving about these teachings and summarized prophetic accounts, he could ask the People of the Book who faithfully continue to read their earlier scripture. It does not imply that the Prophet actually doubted. Such conditional speech may address one who is certain, in order to show that a matter has several mutually supporting proofs: if someone doubts one proof, another remains available.

The Qurʾan has made these teachings clear through arguments reason cannot deny and through accounts displaying God’s way with creation. The earlier scriptures likewise attest the creation, Resurrection, the one divine religion brought by all messengers, humanity’s division into believers and deniers, and God’s decisive judgment between them. These are matters the People of the Book could not deny, although they denied the Prophet’s glad tidings, teachings distinctive to Islam, and particulars they had altered in their books.

This also explains why the present accounts omit Hūd and Ṣāliḥ, whose stories were not in the Torah available to them, and Jethro and Christ, concerning whom the People of the Book disagreed. The argument uses only what they could not repudiate, resembling: Is it not a sign for them that the learned of the Children of Israel recognize it? (42:197). The chapter’s early Meccan setting, before the later Medinan intensification of conflict with the People of the Book, accords with this appeal. In light of this and related verses affirming the revealed truth, the Prophet’s clear insight, and humanity’s inability to produce the like of the Qurʾan, Al-Mizan finds no need for the other proposed explanations.
verses.95:
Al-Mizan holds that after forbidding doubt and hesitation, the verse forbids denying God’s signs. Since an āya is a sign only when its implication and message are clear, its denial amounts to obstinate defiance of truth and arrogance toward God.

“Then you shall be among the losers” states the inevitable consequence of such denial and is, in effect, the central warning: do not become losers. Khasr literally signifies diminution or loss of capital; here the lost capital is faith in God and His signs, the basis of human happiness in this world and the next.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses elucidate the preceding prohibition of denying God’s signs. Their contextual sense is: do not be among the deniers, for deniers do not believe and consequently become losers, since faith is the key to happiness. The wording “those against whom your Lord’s judgment has become due” replaces “the deniers” in order to disclose the basis of their loss: God’s judgment has become due against them, and all affairs ultimately belong to Him.

This judgment is the general law announced to Adam, his wife, and their progeny: We said, ‘Get down from it, all together! Yet, should any guidance come to you from Me, those who follow My guidance shall have no fear, nor shall they grieve. But those who are faithless and deny Our signs, they shall be the inmates of the Fire and they shall remain therein forever (2:39). Thus the deniers, by their disbelief and denial of the signs, incur the word of eternal punishment. They lose faith—the capital of their happiness—and its blessings in this world and the Hereafter.

Once this decree has become due, they cannot believe even if every sign comes to them, until they see the painful punishment. Such compelled belief then brings no benefit. Al-Mizan concludes that obstinate denial makes the verdict of eternal punishment due; that faith is the capital of life’s happiness; and that every person will ultimately believe, either through accepted, voluntary faith that yields happiness here and hereafter, or through unaccepted, forced faith upon seeing the punishment.
verses.97:

Their contextual sense is: do not be among the deniers, for deniers do not believe and consequently become losers, since faith is the key to happiness. verses.98:
Al-Mizan takes “Why has there not been any town that might believe?” as an exhortation to correct, voluntary faith, as shown by “so that its belief might benefit it.” Because the exhortation concerns something past that did not occur, it conveys despair of such belief and functions as a negation: no town believed in time except the people of Jonah.

The meaning is that among the towns whose messengers were denied, none believed voluntarily before punishment descended so that its faith could benefit it, except Jonah’s people. When they believed, God removed the worldly punishment of humiliation and let them enjoy life until the end of their ordinary natural lifespans. The exception is continuous: Jonah’s people belong to the category from which they are excepted.

Al-Mizan rejects readings that make the verse mean either that Jonah’s people alone believed unanimously without a single dissenter, or that it merely states the unusual possibility that a disbelieving town may later believe and benefit from that faith. Though neither sense is intrinsically untenable, the wording does not support their particular implications.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan explains that had God wished all people on earth to believe, they would have done so; but He did not will universal belief, and thus it should neither be expected nor pursued through compulsion. The faith God wills is acquired through a person’s free choice of good, not through coercion.

The rhetorical question, “Would you then force people until they become faithful?” is therefore a denial and prohibition of forcing faith. Since God did not will that everyone believe irrespective of free choice, the Prophet has no authority to compel them, and God does not accept faith produced by such coercion.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse further clarifies God’s exclusive dominion. No cause, including the cause through which a soul freely believes and is guided, can operate and produce its effect except by God’s leave. Thus “No soul may have faith except by Allah’s leave” is a universal and essential rule: the soul’s capacity for faith depends on God’s permission.

God withholds this permission from obstinate unbelievers by placing spiritual impurity and misguidance upon them, leaving them no prospect of happiness. “He lays defilement on those who do not apply reason” removes their capacity to receive that permission, while leaving it for others.

Here rajs, “defilement,” is the opposite of īmān in the form of shakk and rayb, doubt and suspicion, as its juxtaposition with faith indicates. The phrase “those who do not apply reason” denotes the deniers of God’s signs, against whom punishment has become due because God has sealed their hearts, so that they do not understand.
verses.101: Al-Mizan explains the command to observe the heavens and earth as a call to consider their diverse, scattered creations, each of which is a divine sign inviting faith. It appears that mā in mā tughnī al-āyāt wa al-nudhur ʿan qawmin la yuʾminūn is interrogative, making the clause a rhetorical question of denial and despair: what effect can signs and warnings have on people resolved not to believe because their hearts have been sealed? Mā may also be read as a negation, meaning that neither signs nor warnings avail a people without faith.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan connects this verse to the preceding assertion that signs and warnings do not benefit those without faith. Since they wholly disbelieve, they await only days like those of the former nations: the divine punishment that will distinguish the Prophet from them and destroy them, for the sentence of punishment has become due against them.

The command, “Then wait! I too am waiting along with you,” tells them to await that Day of Punishment. It will separate them from the Prophet and make them believe, but their belief then will not benefit them. The initial question is rhetorical and has the force of denial.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains that “Then We shall deliver Our messengers and those who have faith” completes the thought, “Do they await anything except the like of the days of those who passed away before them?” Its underlying sequence is that the Prophet’s people await the days of former nations against whom punishment became due, after which God delivers His messengers and believers. “Say, ‘Then wait! I too am waiting along with you’” intervenes because it answers their awaiting with the Prophet’s own awaiting.

The Prophet’s waiting concerns the judgment between himself and the disbelievers, whereas the subsequent deliverance is not confined to him but includes the believers. Moreover, the main purpose is to warn and frighten the polytheists, rather than to announce deliverance to the Prophet and believers.

“Thus it is a must for Us” (ḥaqqan ʿalaynā) means that just as God delivered the messengers and believers of earlier nations when punishment came, He will deliver the believers of this nation. The definite “the faithful” identifies the believers of the Prophet’s community, and the statement is a divine promise to them and to the Prophet.

Al-Mizan considers it not far-fetched that “to deliver the faithful” subtly indicates that the Prophet will not witness this judgment, but that it will occur after his death. This is suggested by the mention of believers without the Prophet, although messengers and believers were mentioned together in the earlier cases, and may also be inferred from verses such as Whether We show you a part of what We promise them, or take you away, they will be brought back to Us (40:77).
verses.104:
Al-Mizan explains dīn as the practical way of life by which one seeks happiness; it can also denote obedience and, at times, recompense. Doubt about the Prophet’s religion concerns either whether he truly believes in and will remain steadfast upon the path to which he calls, or ignorance of the religion and its principles. The idolaters hoped to turn him from monotheism so as to escape his rejection of idol-worship; he is therefore commanded to declare unequivocally that he worships none of their gods, but Allah alone.

Allah is described as the One who causes them to die because idolaters worshipped their gods in hope of warding off harm and gaining benefit, whereas death—an unavoidable harm—is exclusively in God’s power. The description also carries a veiled threat: their death is the appointed time of the punishment promised to deniers. Its connection with the command to be among the faithful indicates the contrasting promise that God delivers believers from punishment. The Prophet thus declares both his dissociation from false gods and his worship of the God who punishes deniers and delivers the faithful.

The command to “Set your countenance upon the religion, as a hanif” continues what the Prophet is commanded to say: he has been commanded to be among the faithful, to direct himself to the religion as a hanif, and never to be among the polytheists.

verses.106:
Al-Mizan regards this as a further prohibition of idol-worship: invoking other than Allah makes one a wrongdoer and thus liable to the promised consequence for wrongdoers. The phrase “that which neither benefits you nor can do you any harm” itself supplies the reason for the prohibition.

The commentary notes that objects of worship in (10:104) are called “those” (alladhīna), since worshippers naturally conceive their objects of worship as possessing sense and intellect. Here the objects of invocation are instead called “that” (mā), a term fitting inanimate things. Although invocation is also worship, this wording refutes the possible thought that such objects possess intelligence and can benefit or harm: they are inanimate and cannot be conceived as doing either.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains this conditional statement as continuing the prohibition against invoking things other than God. If Allah afflicts someone with distress, none but Him can remove it; if He intends good for someone, none can prevent His grace. He is therefore dominant over all others, grants good to whichever servants He wills, and is Forgiving and Merciful toward them. Since God alone possesses these qualities, while all others lack them, He alone must be worshipped and invoked.
verses.108: Al-Mizan identifies “the truth” as the Qurʾan or its teachings. The verse leaves people free to choose, while stating the reality decreed by God: whoever is guided by the truth receives its benefit for his own soul, and whoever strays bears its harm himself. The Prophet is not their guardian who averts from them what is against them. The verse consequently implies that they must be guided to the truth, because their benefit lies in it.
verses.109: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to follow the revelation and patiently endure the hardships and trials that arise from doing so. God will judge between him and his people, and His judgment will bring the Prophet joy. The verse therefore enjoins steadfastness in calling to the truth, consoles him for his suffering, and promises him a good end. It concludes the chapter by invoking God’s judgment, which is the subject that most of its verses seek to explain.
